name: South-Central Dravidian
region: Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, and the Gond and Kui–Kuvi areas of central and eastern India
defining_innovation: Apical displacement: an initial vowel was lost and a following r, l or ḍ moved to the front of the word, so Proto-Dravidian *iraṇṭu 'two' is Telugu reṇḍu, against Tamil iraṇṭu.

chapters.title: Origins
chapters.body: South-Central Dravidian includes Telugu, with more than 80 million speakers the largest Dravidian language, and a string of tribal languages across central India: Gondi, Konda, Kui, Kuvi and Pengo. Bhadriraju Krishnamurti, himself a Telugu speaker, defined the branch by a sound change he called **apical displacement**. In words like `*iraṇṭu` 'two', the initial vowel disappeared and the tongue-tip consonant moved forward: Telugu *reṇḍu*, against Tamil *iraṇṭu*.

chapters.title: Telugu
chapters.body: Telugu words appear in Prakrit inscriptions from the last centuries BCE, and the first inscription wholly in Telugu dates to the 6th century CE. Its literature begins with **Nannaya**'s Telugu rendering of the *Mahābhārata* in the 11th century, written in a highly Sanskritised style. Telugu script developed, like Kannada script, from a southern form of Brahmi, and the two scripts remain closely related. In 2008 India declared Telugu a 'classical language', together with Kannada.

turning_points.title: Apical displacement
turning_points.description: Word-initial vowels drop and a following apical consonant moves to the start of the word: `*iraṇṭu` 'two' → Telugu *reṇḍu*. Krishnamurti's identification of this change was a landmark in Dravidian comparative phonology. Its date is uncertain.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju. 2003. The Dravidian Languages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

turning_points.title: Telugu inscriptions
turning_points.description: After centuries of Telugu words appearing in Prakrit and Sanskrit inscriptions, the first inscriptions wholly in Telugu appear, in a script derived from southern Brahmi.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju. 2003. The Dravidian Languages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

turning_points.title: Nannaya and Sanskrit
turning_points.description: Nannaya's Telugu *Mahābhārata* begins Telugu literature in a style full of Sanskrit vocabulary. The gap between this literary register and everyday speech lasts until 20th-century reformers push for a written language closer to speech.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju. 2003. The Dravidian Languages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

turning_points.title: Classical language status
turning_points.description: The Government of India declares Telugu a classical language, recognising its antiquity and literary tradition and funding its study. Meanwhile, the tribal South-Central languages such as Gondi and Kui are losing speakers to regional languages.

sources.citation: Steever, Sanford B., ed. 2020. The Dravidian Languages, 2nd ed. London: Routledge.
